## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Aḍḍhakāsitherīgāthā* (Thig 2.4) is a short poem of two verses (verses 25–26) in the *Therīgāthā* of the Khuddaka Nikāya [Blackstone 2000]. The verses are spoken by the elder nun Aḍḍhakāsī, one of several former courtesans mentioned in early Buddhist literature who renounced worldly life and attained arahantship [Young 2004; Horner 1930]. In the poem, she recalls her past profession, stating that her earnings were as high as the revenue of the realm of Kāsī, before detailing her disgust and disaffection with the physical body, leading to her renunciation, spiritual practice, and the attainment of the three knowledges [Blackstone 2000].

Narrative literature, including the *Apadāna* and the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, contextualizes her life story within karmic causality, relating that her rebirth as a courtesan arose from an insult directed at an arahant nun during the dispensation of Kassapa Buddha [Young 2004; Schober 1997].

 Within Pali literature, DharmaNexus detects text reuse primarily in the *Therīgāthā-aṭṭhakathā*, which quotes and glosses the verses, and shared formulaic phrases with the *Theragāthā-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
